topics.title: Hot Carrier Solar Cell
topics.description: Hot-carrier solar cells aim to reduce energy loss by extracting photoexcited carriers before they cool to the band edges. Our research explores two-dimensional van der Waals materials, ultrafast carrier dynamics, energy-selective contacts, and interface engineering to develop photovoltaic devices that exceed the conventional Shockley–Queisser limit.
topics.long_description:
In conventional solar cells, photons with energies higher than the semiconductor bandgap generate energetic electrons and holes. However, these “hot” carriers rapidly lose their excess energy through carrier–phonon scattering and relax to the band edges. This thermalization process represents one of the major energy-loss mechanisms in photovoltaic devices and contributes to the Shockley–Queisser efficiency limit of conventional single-junction solar cells.

Hot-carrier solar cells aim to minimize this loss by extracting photoexcited carriers before they fully cool. Achieving this requires materials with sufficiently long hot-carrier lifetimes, reduced carrier-cooling rates, efficient carrier transport, and energy-selective contacts that allow high-energy carriers to be collected without significant loss of voltage.

Our research investigates two-dimensional materials and van der Waals heterostructures as promising platforms for hot-carrier photovoltaics. Their atomically thin structure, strong light–matter interaction, tunable electronic properties, clean interfaces, and unusual carrier–phonon interactions provide opportunities to control hot-carrier generation, cooling, transport, and extraction. We study graphene, transition-metal dichalcogenides, and related low-dimensional materials to understand how their electronic structure and interfacial properties influence non-equilibrium carrier dynamics.

A major focus of our work is the engineering of ultraclean contacts, tunnelling interfaces, graphene-based intermediate electrodes, and energy-selective extraction layers. By combining optical spectroscopy, electrical transport, quantum-efficiency measurements, device modelling, and ultrafast carrier-dynamics studies, we aim to establish the physical mechanisms required for efficient hot-carrier collection.

Our long-term objective is to develop practical photovoltaic architectures that suppress thermalization losses, preserve the excess energy of photoexcited carriers, and achieve power-conversion efficiencies beyond the conventional Shockley–Queisser limit.

topics.title: Multiple Exiton Generation
topics.description: Multiple exciton generation enables a single high-energy photon to produce two or more electron–hole pairs, increasing photocurrent and reducing energy loss. Our research explores carrier multiplication and singlet-fission-assisted exciton generation in two-dimensional materials and van der Waals heterostructures to develop photovoltaic devices that exceed the conventional Shockley–Queisser limit.
topics.long_description:
In conventional solar cells, the absorption of one photon typically generates one electron–hole pair, while photon energy exceeding the semiconductor bandgap is rapidly lost through carrier cooling. Multiple exciton generation, also known as carrier multiplication, offers a route to utilize this excess energy by allowing a single high-energy photon to generate two or more electron–hole pairs. This process can enhance photocurrent and increase photovoltaic efficiency beyond the conventional Shockley–Queisser limit.

Our research investigates multiple exciton generation in two-dimensional semiconductors and van der Waals heterostructures. Strong Coulomb interactions, reduced dielectric screening, tunable electronic structures, and atomically sharp interfaces make these materials promising platforms for efficient carrier multiplication and ultrafast energy transfer.

We explore both intrinsic carrier multiplication and sensitized approaches based on singlet exciton fission. In hybrid organic–two-dimensional material systems, one high-energy singlet exciton can split into two lower-energy triplet excitons, which can subsequently transfer their energy or charge to an adjacent semiconductor. This provides a potential route to increase exciton yield and improve the utilization of high-energy photons.

A major focus of our work is understanding the competition between exciton multiplication, carrier cooling, interfacial transfer, and recombination. By combining ultrafast spectroscopy, optical characterization, electrical measurements, and device engineering, we aim to identify materials and interfaces that enable efficient generation, separation, and collection of multiple excitons.

Our long-term objective is to integrate multiple exciton generation with optimized contacts and photovoltaic architectures to develop solar cells with enhanced photocurrent and efficiencies beyond those of conventional single-junction devices.

topics.title: Quantum Nano-Photonics and Polariton Physics
topics.description: Our research explores quantum nanophotonics and polariton physics in two-dimensional materials and van der Waals heterostructures. By controlling excitons, photons, optical cavities, and nanoscale electromagnetic fields, we aim to manipulate light–matter interactions and develop new platforms for quantum optoelectronics, energy conversion, sensing, and photonic technologies.
topics.long_description:
Quantum nanophotonics investigates the interaction of light with matter at nanometre length scales, where optical confinement and quantum effects can strongly modify absorption, emission, and energy transport. Two-dimensional materials are particularly attractive for this field because they host strongly bound excitons, large optical oscillator strengths, tunable electronic structures, and atomically thin interfaces that can be integrated with a wide range of photonic structures.

Our research focuses on controlling light–matter interactions in two-dimensional materials and van der Waals heterostructures using optical microcavities, nanophotonic resonators, dielectric environments, reflective electrodes, and plasmonic structures. These approaches allow us to enhance and tailor optical absorption, emission, exciton dynamics, and energy transfer at the nanoscale.

A major area of interest is exciton–polariton physics. Exciton–polaritons are hybrid quasiparticles formed through strong coupling between excitons in a semiconductor and confined photons in an optical cavity. They combine the strong interactions of matter with the low effective mass and coherence of light, enabling phenomena such as enhanced energy transport, nonlinear optical response, polariton condensation, and coherent light–matter dynamics.

We investigate how cavity design, material thickness, dielectric screening, temperature, excitation density, and interfacial coupling influence polariton formation and behaviour. Particular attention is given to room-temperature strong coupling, interlayer excitons, polariton-assisted energy transfer, and the modification of carrier generation and recombination through optical-field confinement.

By combining nanophotonic design, optical spectroscopy, device fabrication, and two-dimensional material engineering, our long-term objective is to develop polaritonic and nanophotonic platforms for quantum light sources, low-threshold emitters, optical sensing, integrated photonics, and advanced photovoltaic and optoelectronic energy-conversion devices.

topics.title: Contact Engineering and Device Physics
topics.description: Contact engineering is essential for controlling charge injection, extraction, recombination, and energy loss in two-dimensional devices. Our research develops ultraclean van der Waals contacts, tunnelling interfaces, and optimized device architectures to improve carrier transport and the performance of photovoltaic and optoelectronic devices.
topics.long_description:
The performance of two-dimensional electronic, photovoltaic, and optoelectronic devices is strongly influenced by the interfaces between the semiconductor, electrodes, and surrounding materials. Conventional metal deposition can introduce defects, chemical disorder, strain, contamination, and Fermi-level pinning, resulting in large contact resistance, leakage current, carrier recombination, and reduced device efficiency.

Our research focuses on developing clean and controlled contact strategies for two-dimensional semiconductors and van der Waals heterostructures. These include transferred metal contacts, van der Waals electrodes, graphene intermediate layers, ultrathin tunnelling barriers, and dielectric interface engineering. Such approaches can preserve the intrinsic properties of atomically thin materials while enabling efficient carrier injection and extraction.

We investigate how contact materials, interface states, band alignment, barrier height, tunnelling processes, and electrode geometry determine device behaviour. Particular attention is given to Schottky-barrier formation, Fermi-level pinning, defect-assisted tunnelling, contact resistance, dark-current suppression, carrier selectivity, and interfacial recombination.

Our device-physics studies combine current–voltage measurements, temperature-dependent transport, capacitance analysis, photocurrent mapping, quantum-efficiency measurements, optical spectroscopy, and numerical modelling. These methods allow us to understand the relationship between microscopic interface properties and macroscopic device performance.

The long-term objective is to establish reliable contact and interface designs for high-efficiency solar cells, photodetectors, transistors, and other low-dimensional optoelectronic devices.

topics.title: Quantum Optoelectronic Devices
topics.description: Our research develops quantum optoelectronic devices based on two-dimensional materials and van der Waals heterostructures. By controlling light–matter interaction, excitons, charge transfer, and quantum confinement, we aim to create high-performance photodetectors, light-emitting devices, photovoltaic systems, and other emerging quantum photonic technologies.
topics.long_description:
Quantum optoelectronic devices use the interaction between light and quantum-confined electronic states to generate, detect, manipulate, or convert optical signals. Two-dimensional materials and van der Waals heterostructures offer an exceptional platform for such devices because of their strong light–matter interaction, reduced dimensionality, tunable band structures, tightly bound excitons, and atomically sharp interfaces.

Our research investigates how excitons, free carriers, interlayer charge transfer, quantum confinement, and interface effects determine the optical and electrical response of low-dimensional devices. By selecting suitable material combinations and controlling layer thickness, stacking order, band alignment, dielectric environment, and electrode geometry, we aim to tailor the generation, transport, and recombination of photoexcited carriers.

We develop and study photovoltaic devices, photodetectors, light-emitting structures, tunnelling devices, and hybrid quantum optoelectronic systems. Particular emphasis is placed on improving responsivity, sensitivity, spectral selectivity, response speed, emission efficiency, and energy-conversion performance while reducing dark current and non-radiative recombination.

Our work also explores advanced light–matter coupling concepts, including exciton–polariton formation, optical-cavity integration, plasmonic enhancement, and field-controlled optoelectronic behaviour. These approaches provide opportunities to manipulate optical absorption, emission, and carrier dynamics beyond the limits of conventional semiconductor devices.

By combining device fabrication, optical spectroscopy, electrical transport, photocurrent mapping, and interface engineering, our long-term goal is to establish new quantum optoelectronic architectures for sensing, imaging, communication, energy conversion, and integrated photonic technologies.
